Lineup: Surfing and Subculture by John Witzig

(Gra Murdoch)
Swellnet Dispatch
Tuesday, 22 September 2026
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 10:22
Instaread

In one of my boxes of keepsakes, there’s a yellowing old colour print that I treasure more than most. I’m looking at it now. It’s of my mates, between surfs, on a hot northerly day in Johanna, maybe around ’85. Azza’s blue Kombi’s parked, roof popped up. Dicko’s leaning on the passenger seat, chatting with Hamish. Johnny’s in the footwell of the sliding side door, lost in thought. Azza, Monty and Thomsy are sprawled out on the grass on scattered towels. Cam, who’s new to surfing, and owner of the slightly incongruous mal in the foreground, is sitting a little apart from the pack, grinning at Thomsy, who’s taking the piss out of the whole thing by fixing me with a stare and theatrically grabbing his balls.

I look at the photo and I can feel the dry Victorian heat, and that delicious reward – the widescreen conjuror’s trick – of driving away from a flat, devil-winded Surf Coast and emerging ‘Down South’ out the other side of Cape Otway to a roaring offshore world. 

I’m pretty sure this photo is the day after three or four of us stepped out of the Anglesea Pub around 11.00pm, sniffed the nor’east wind and decided to drive Down South there and then, packing bongs between Great Ocean Road curves along the way. We got to Joey around 2:00am and crashed out on the grass under a big bright moon, all lined up in a row like snags on a barbecue. Azza slept in the Kombi of course. Last thing I remember before collapsing was Johnny, faux annoyed, asking if someone could please turn the moon down. The rest of the crew followed us down the next morning after a more conventional night’s sleep. 

I can’t remember the waves we scored on this occasion. It might have mattered then, it doesn’t matter now. Not as much as the adventure. Not as much as the mates.

Back in 2014, John Witzig had an exhibition at the National Portrait Gallery in Canberra. Curated by Sarah Engledow and titled Arcadia, sound of the sea, it was complemented by Nicholas Harding’s ink drawings and trippy footage courtesy of Albe Falzon. After a quick regional tour (Geelong and the Tweed), John’s prints – some well over two metres wide – were laid down to hibernate out in the shed at his North Coast haven.

Grafton Regional Gallery came calling some time in 2025. John went out to the shed, grabbed one of the packs small enough to fit in his car and drove to G-town. Together with, GRG Director Jane Kreis and acting curator Cass Samms, they opened up the package and the prints inside looked to be in immaculate condition.

A truck was dispatched and the rest of the prints were brought in. All turned out to be as well preserved as when they were packed by the Portrait Gallery crew in 2014. No small achievement, when you think of the lurches in atmosphere from one scorching / humid / torrential extreme to the next over any given decade, not to mention the 2019 fires that came within twenty metres of John’s shed.

Arcadia, 1969 (John Witzig)

John’s exhibition, Lineup: Surfing and Subculture exhibition launched in July this year. The title’s a bit misleading, really. There’s two or three ‘surf shots’ in total, and a similar number of lineups. The rest of it is people. And while they do represent a subculture, in reality they were, and are, John’s mates, captured between ’63 and ’78 (about the same span of time that the prints would later lay undisturbed in his shed, come to think of it).

It’s a simple, striking, beautiful exhibition, in a modest and lovely gallery space. Unframed prints (archival pigment on 310 gsm Canson Platine Fibre Rag) pinned to walls, given room to breathe. Mostly black and white. 

Like many, I’m far too attached to my phone these days. I consume my surf media on screens large and small. I’d forgotten how meditative and affirming it is to be in a gallery, and to have a kind of quiet convo with what’s been placed there for me to look at.

(Gra Murdoch)

Anyway, last Saturday, we were there to hear John in conversation with Robert Moore, a notable Clarence Valley Artist. We – a full house of mellow, mostly silver haired nostalgists – took our seats.

‘In Conversation With’s often strain under the weight of artifice, but Robert did a valiant job. John’s laconic, honest and wry humour both grounds and elevates most conversations he’s part of. 

It never hurts to run through someone’s bio. We learnt about John’s architectural education; the influence of the European photography magazine TWEN (where black and white was king); how his learning and technical journey has always been intuitive; how in ’63 he had his first story published in SW; how in ’66 he was given the reins to produce an entire issue himself, and how that led, in ’71 to him, Albe Falzon and David Elfick launching Tracks; how he and Albe rotated editing duties, allowing John to spend every second month in Angourie, and freeing Alby to make Morning of the Earth.

We learnt how John’s trips across the Nullarbor – via Cactus, of course – south to Margies and as far north as Kalbarri, were the best and purest surfing adventures of his life. “I like surfing, surfing is fun, but I like the adventures most.” 

Robert Moore, at left, and John Witzig in conversation - as a youthful Ted Spencer looks on (Gra Murdoch)

It’s quite a clue in that statement. Surfing was ‘fun’ for John, but it wasn’t ‘everything’ to him, like it can be for many of us, (especially those frothing first few decades). Literally and metaphorically, John was always willing and able to look away from the riding of waves and look around instead. And that’s where the magic lay.

Being genuinely keen to throw some well-deserved bouquets John’s way, Robert kept trying to direct the conversation into artspeak territory, speaking of the cultural significance of the portraiture, the sophistication of his eye for composition, etc., but John was having none of it – kindly and gently laughing it off with, “Robert, you make it all sound more important than it was!”

This is no false modesty on John’s part. John simply said he found standing on the beach shooting surfing action a bit boring, as there was so much more happening than just the wave riding act. Being a magazine editor, he took the sort of photos he’d want to see as an editor – photos that would tell a story. No big deal. It was magic, sure, but there was no sorcery involved.

A house at Torquay, 1970 (John Witzig) 

John then motioned to two photos to his right: a nice Bells lineup, and a photo of a young Stephen Cooney perched in the door of a Kombi, mug of tea in hand, and said, “That lineup shows Bells, Stephen turning up for a cup of tea, that’s what it’s like to be at Bells.”

That was as close as John got to declaring some kind of Artist’s Statement, before continuing, “Everyone on the walls here was a good friend of mine, I didn’t take photos of people I didn’t like.” And when asked to reflect on the significance of documenting this Northern Rivers counter-culture, John simply shrugged and said, “I was just documenting my own life.”

Good on Robert for trying to give the convo some artistic gravitas, but the thing about John is, A) he’s aware of his place in the pantheon; B) he regards the pantheon something not to be taken too seriously anyway, C) he recognises the right-place-right-time circumstance that plugged him into the original cast of the Country Soul surfing dream, and D) he’s too accomplished to stray within coo-ee of high-falutin’ art-speak territory anyway.

Case in point: there’s a really great image I had never actually seen until yesterday. Shot at the Bells Easter comp in ’75. Shot from the Rincon cliff, back to Bells, it shows Bugs with a couple of clean looking pintails under arm, striding up the stairs through a time-capsule crowd of hair, bell bottoms, beards and double denim. Robert rhapsodised about the sophistication of the image, how shots like can’t simply be "snapped" ad hoc without premeditation and preparation, and how unlikely it is for someone to simply spin around and ‘snap’ such a picture. To which John replied that, ahhh, spinning around and snapping the picture is pretty much what he actually did … before granting that, well, he anticipated the moment somewhat, and ‘had the good sense’ to depress the shutter at the right moment.

Bells steps, 1977 (John Witzig)

Part of the magic of this collection lies, of course, in the era it documents: the woollen jumpers, the hair, the cars, the verandahs, the quiet lineups, a startlingly good-looking coterie of surf-fit mates, the absence of logos. All of it so natural, effortlessly cool, seemingly innocent, emanating joy and contentment. It’s little wonder that half a century later many of us crave and imitate the aesthetic still.

Being a former magazine hack myself, one of my favourite yarns in the chat was John talking about his dealing with surf magazines. In the pre-digital day, it was a great, and often betrayed, leap of faith for photographers to post their treasured transparencies to magazines here and overseas. One of John’s mightiest images – North Coast couple with baby, kitchen table loaded with an abundance of veggies that’d have Rasta envious – was sent to SURFER magazine and vanished in the archives, never to return – until decades later, when Jeff Divine, photo editing for The Surfers Journal by then, emailed John – subject title “Look what I’ve found.” The precious transparency found its way home.

But as they say, you can only keep what you have by giving it away. And John’s donated this collection of outrageously well-printed images, huge in scale and heart and stoke – to the Grafton gallery. The exhibition is open for a week or so more, hopefully longer. Maybe the show will tour. If it does, do your best to get there and take your time standing in front of these prints. If nothing else, you’ll come away thinking of the mates you’ve shared the best of times with.

//GRA MURDOCH

Visit Johnwitzig.com.au

benskii Wednesday, 23 Sep 2026 at 09:50 am new

Brilliant write up, Gra, thank you. I hope the exhibition makes its way north to the sunny coast. 

I'm too young for that era but gees I love the imagery and what seems to be something we'll never have again in surfing. 

One thing I love about it is how it's before the surf industry. So I imagine the woollen jumpers and jeans are what everyone was wearing, surfing and non surfers alike. If that's the case, then I imagine the surf culture was formed around the act of surfing and the people who did it. Whereas today, the culture is more of a top down influence, with companies selling us clothing and ideals in the imagery, that informs the way we interact and the images that define us. 

A write up of a young surfer in a mainstream surf mag these days seems just as much a promotional opportunity for the sponsors as a get to know someone who'll influence the culture. But back then, as he said, John was just taking pictures of his mates. Beautiful. 

I think that's what I appreciate that the most. No one in the pictures is trying to sell us anything. It's just documenting the emergence of something that would become a part of mainstream Australian life. I do hope there's someone out there doing the same today. For the current "underground" or un-sponsored surf culture, and for whatever else is the counter culture of today that old folk like most of us aren't aware of yet. 

It's also interesting to think about what might have been if a different set of people got into surfing. What would our surf culture look like today if it was a bunch of clubbies from Sydney who dominated surfing and set the tone with their military style discipline at the time. Would the photos in the Grafton gallery look like they do or would the counter culture crew have taken up something else?  Pointless musings really but it adds to the gratitude I feel towards those guys for stepping outside the norm and laying the foundations for us to enjoy today. 

No doubt they would disagree but I think we owe them a lot for the joy we get in this little pastime of ours.
